Inversion ($V_G > V_T$): $E_{Fi}$ at the surface falls below $E_F$, electrons form an n-type channel, $\phi_s = 2\phi_{fp}$ at threshold.

(iii) Calculate the threshold voltage of a MOSFET having gate-oxide thickness $t_{ox} = 1$ nm and flat-band voltage $V_{FB} = 1.0$ V. (iv) What gate voltage is needed to form the maximum inversion-layer charge?
questions.method: $\phi_{fp} = V_t\ln(N_A/n_i)$; $x_{dT} = (4\epsilon_s\phi_{fp}/eN_A)^{1/2}$; $|Q'_{SD}| = eN_Ax_{dT}$; $|Q'_I| = \epsilon_{ox}E_{ox} - |Q'_{SD}|$; electrons $= |Q'_I|LW/e$; $V_T = V_{FB} + 2\phi_{fp} + |Q'_{SD}|/C_{ox}$; $V_G = V_T + |Q'_I|/C_{ox}$ ($N_A$ printed $5^{18}$, read $5\times10^{18}$).
draws: Diagram: MOS charges at the maximum inversion charge with the Gauss balance

questions.label: 18-19 3(b)
questions.text: What are the parameters that affect the magnitude of threshold voltage in a MOSFET?
questions.points: $V_{TN} = (|Q'_{SD}(\max)| - Q'_{ss})t_{ox}/\epsilon_{ox} + \phi_{ms} + 2\phi_{fp}$: substrate doping (through $\phi_{fp}$ and $Q'_{SD}$), oxide thickness and permittivity, fixed oxide charge $Q'_{ss}$, gate material (work function difference $\phi_{ms}$), temperature, body bias (body effect), ion implant adjustment.
draws: Graph: threshold voltage against substrate doping for several oxide thicknesses

questions.label: 18-19 3(c)
questions.text: What is body effect of MOSFET?
questions.points: A reverse source-to-body bias $V_{SB}$ widens the depletion region under the gate, adding bulk charge, so more gate voltage is needed: $\Delta V_T = \gamma(\sqrt{2\phi_{fp} + V_{SB}} - \sqrt{2\phi_{fp}})$, $\gamma = \sqrt{2e\epsilon_sN_a}/C_{ox}$ (body-effect coefficient). Matters in stacked transistors.
draws: Graph: threshold voltage against source-to-body voltage
Diagram: depletion region with and without body bias

questions.label: 18-19 3(d)
questions.text: Explain the amplification action of a transistor.
questions.points: Forward-biased B-E junction injects electrons that cross the thin base and are swept into the collector; $i_C = I_Se^{v_{BE}/V_t}$, so a small $v_{be}$ makes a large change in $i_C$; through $R_C$ this gives $v_{ce} = -g_mR_Cv_{be}$, voltage gain $A_v = -I_CR_C/V_t$; current gain $\beta = i_C/i_B$.
draws: Circuit: common-emitter amplifier
Graph: input and output waveforms of the amplifier

questions.label: 19-20 5(b)
questions.text: Find ideal pn junction current and sketch ideal electron and hole current components.
questions.outline: $n_{p0} = n_{n0}e^{-eV_{bi}/kT}$; barrier $V_{bi} - V_a$ gives the law of the junction $p_n(x_n) = p_{n0}e^{eV_a/kT}$, $n_p(-x_p) = n_{p0}e^{eV_a/kT}$; minority diffusion equations; decaying exponentials; diffusion currents at the edges; add: $J = [eD_pp_{n0}/L_p + eD_nn_{p0}/L_n](e^{eV_a/kT} - 1)$; majority currents make up the rest.
draws: Graph: minority carrier distributions on both sides of a forward-biased junction
Graph: electron, hole and total current against position

questions.label: 18-19 4(a)
questions.text: Sketch the ideal electron and hole current components through a $pn$ junction under forward bias.
questions.points: Minority diffusion currents $J_p(x_n)$ and $J_n(-x_p)$ at the space charge edges decay as $e^{-(x - x_n)/L_p}$ into the neutral regions; the majority currents rise to keep the total $J$ constant everywhere; no recombination in the space charge region.
draws: Graph: electron and hole current densities through a forward-biased pn junction
compare: Minority vs majority current: diffusion, decays over $L$ vs makes up the constant total

questions.label: 18-19 4(b)
questions.text: What are the factors which cause base current in a transistor?
questions.points: Holes injected from the base into the emitter ($I_{pE}$, emitter injection efficiency); recombination of electrons in the base ($I_{RB}$, base transport factor); recombination in the B-E space charge region ($I_R$); minus the reverse B-C leakage $I_{CBO}$.
draws: Diagram: current components in an npn transistor in active mode

questions.label: 19-20 1(d)
questions.text: Explain Schottky barrier. How it differs from ohmic contact? Explain.
questions.points: Metal on n-type with $\phi_m > \phi_s$: electrons leave the semiconductor, a depletion layer and upward band bending form a barrier $\phi_{B0} = \phi_m - \chi$, $V_{bi} = \phi_{B0} - \phi_n$; current by thermionic emission $J = J_{sT}(e^{eV_a/kT} - 1)$, rectifying, majority carriers, fast. Ohmic contact: $\phi_m < \phi_s$ (accumulation, no barrier) or a heavily doped surface so electrons tunnel; linear I-V, negligible resistance.
draws: Diagram: metal and n-type band diagrams before and after contact
Diagram: ohmic contact band diagram
Graph: I-V of rectifying and ohmic contacts
compare: Schottky barrier vs ohmic contact: depletion, barrier, thermionic emission, rectifying vs accumulation or tunneling, no barrier, linear

questions.label: 18-19 4(c)
questions.text: Differentiate between ohmic and rectifying contacts.
questions.points: Rectifying (Schottky): $\phi_m > \phi_s$ on n-type, barrier $\phi_{B0} = \phi_m - \chi$, current by thermionic emission one way only, I-V like a diode. Ohmic: low or negative barrier ($\phi_m < \phi_s$ on n-type) or heavy doping so electrons tunnel through a thin barrier; linear I-V, small resistance either way.
draws: Diagram: band diagrams of rectifying and ohmic contacts
Graph: I-V curves of rectifying and ohmic contacts
compare: Ohmic vs rectifying contact: linear, either direction vs barrier, one direction

questions.label: 18-19 6(d)
questions.text: With suitable energy band diagrams, explain Schottky contact.
questions.points: Metal on n-type with $\phi_m > \phi_s$: electrons flow to the metal until $E_F$ is flat, leaving a depletion region and barrier $\phi_{B0} = \phi_m - \chi$, $V_{bi} = \phi_{B0} - \phi_n$. Forward bias lowers $V_{bi}$: thermionic emission $J = A^*T^2e^{-e\phi_{B0}/kT}(e^{eV_a/kT} - 1)$; reverse bias raises it. Majority carriers, no storage, fast switching; Ex 9.1: 0.54 V barrier.
draws: Diagram: metal and n-type band diagrams before and after contact
Diagram: Schottky contact under forward and reverse bias
compare: Schottky vs pn diode: majority carriers, no stored charge, lower turn-on vs minority injection, storage time

questions.label: 18-19 4(d)
questions.text: What is base width modulation?
questions.points: Raising $V_{CE}$ widens the B-C space charge region into the base, so the neutral base width $x_B$ shrinks; the minority gradient and $I_C \propto 1/x_B$ rise; output curves slope and meet at $-V_A$ (Early voltage); also called the Early effect; finite output resistance.
draws: Graph: minority carrier distribution in the base for two collector voltages
Graph: collector current against collector-emitter voltage with the Early voltage

questions.label: 20-21 5(c)
questions.text: Explain the working principle of Tunnel diode. Draw its characteristics curve.
questions.points: Both sides degenerately doped, so $E_F$ lies inside the bands and the depletion layer is only 5 to 17 nm thick; electrons tunnel where filled states face empty ones; the current rises to a peak $I_p$, falls to a valley $I_v$ (negative resistance), then rises as normal diode current; reverse bias tunnels freely.
draws: Diagram: electron wave at a thick and a thin barrier
Diagram: tunnel diode band diagrams at several biases
Graph: tunnel diode I-V curve

questions.label: 18-19 4(e)
questions.text: Explain the working of Tunnel diode. Draw its characteristics curve.
questions.points: Both sides degenerately doped, very thin junction: electrons tunnel between filled n-side states and empty p-side states. Small forward bias: current rises to a peak; more bias: bands uncross, current falls (negative resistance) to a valley; then normal diffusion current. Reverse bias: large tunnelling current.
draws: Diagram: tunnel diode band diagrams at zero bias, peak, valley and reverse bias
Graph: tunnel diode I-V characteristic with peak, valley and negative resistance

questions.label: 18-19 5(a)
questions.text: Describe diffusion process. Derive the expression for diffusion current density.
questions.outline: Carriers move randomly with $v_{th}$ over mean free path $l$; half of those at $\pm l$ cross $x = 0$: $F = \frac12v_{th}[n(-l) - n(+l)]$; Taylor $n(\pm l) = n(0) \pm l\,dn/dx$; $F = -v_{th}l\,dn/dx$; $J_n = -eF = eD_n\,dn/dx$ with $D_n = v_{th}l$; holes $J_p = -eD_p\,dp/dx$; total with drift.
draws: Graph: electron concentration against distance with the flux across $x = 0$

questions.label: 18-19 5(b)
questions.text: Draw the ideal low-frequency capacitance versus gate voltage curve of a MOS capacitor with p-type substrate and indicate different regions.
questions.points: p-type MOS: accumulation ($V_G < V_{FB}$): $C = C_{ox}$; depletion: $C_{ox}$ in series with $C'_{SD} = \epsilon_s/x_d$, falls; minimum $C'_{min}$ at threshold ($x_d = x_{dT}$); low-frequency inversion: inversion charge follows, $C$ returns to $C_{ox}$ (high frequency stays at $C_{min}$).
draws: Graph: ideal low-frequency C-V curve of a p-type MOS capacitor with the three regions
Diagram: charge in accumulation, depletion and inversion

questions.label: 20-21 3(d)
questions.text: For the following questions: (i) Solve the ambipolar transport equation for a semiconductor with $N_a = 5\times10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$ for $x > 0$ at steady state with zero electric field where excess charges are created only at $x = 0$. ($\delta n_0 = 5\times10^{15}$ cm$^{-3}$). (ii) Find the distance where the excess charge will drop to $10\times10^{13}$ cm$^{-3}$. (Assume $\tau_{n0} = 7\times10^{-7}$ s, $\tau_{p0} = 5\times10^{-7}$ s, $D_n = 30$ cm$^2$ s$^{-1}$, $D_p = 25$ cm$^2$ s$^{-1}$) (iii) Plot n and p as function of x in log scale.
questions.method: Low injection in p-type: ambipolar equation becomes $D_n\,\delta n'' - \delta n/\tau_{n0} = 0$; solution decaying for $x > 0$: $\delta n = \delta n_0e^{-x/L_n}$, $L_n = \sqrt{D_n\tau_{n0}}$; solve $\delta n(x) = 10^{14}$ for $x$.
draws: Graph: excess electrons decaying into the bar
Graph: total electron and hole concentrations on a log scale

questions.label: 19-20 5(a)
questions.text: Consider a p-type semiconductor that is homogeneous and infinite in extent. Assume a zero applied electric field. For a one-dimensional crystal, assume that excess carriers are being generated at $x = 0$ only. The excess carriers being generated at $x = 0$ will being *[sic: should be will begin]* diffusing in both the $-x$ and $+x$ directions. Calculate the steady-state excess carrier concentration as a function of $x$.
questions.outline: Ambipolar equation with minority electron parameters; $E = 0$, $g' = 0$ for $x \ne 0$, steady state; $\delta n'' - \delta n/L_n^2 = 0$; $Ae^{-x/L_n} + Be^{x/L_n}$; finite at $\pm\infty$; $\delta n = \delta n(0)e^{-|x|/L_n}$.
draws: Graph: excess carriers decaying on both sides of the source

questions.label: 19-20 TT2 8(a)
questions.text: Consider a p-type semiconductor that is homogeneous and infinite in extent. Assume a zero applied electric field. For a one-dimensional crystal, assume that excess carriers are being generated at $x = 0$ only. The excess carriers being generated at $x = 0$ will begin diffusing in both the $-x$ and $+x$ directions. Calculate the steady-state excess carrier concentration as a function of $x$.
questions.outline: Ambipolar equation with minority electron parameters; $E = 0$, $g' = 0$ for $x \ne 0$, steady state; $\delta n'' - \delta n/L_n^2 = 0$; $Ae^{-x/L_n} + Be^{x/L_n}$; finite at $\pm\infty$; $\delta n = \delta n(0)e^{-|x|/L_n}$.
draws: Graph: excess carriers decaying on both sides of the source

questions.label: 18-19 5(c)
questions.text: Show that diffusion length is the average length a carrier diffuses before recombination.
questions.outline: Steady state, no field: $D_p\,d^2\delta p/dx^2 - \delta p/\tau_{p0} = 0$; $L_p = \sqrt{D_p\tau_{p0}}$; $\delta p = \delta p_0e^{-x/L_p}$; probability of recombining in $dx$: $P(x)dx = (1/L_p)e^{-x/L_p}dx$; mean $\langle x\rangle = (1/L_p)\int_0^\infty xe^{-x/L_p}dx = L_p$ (integration by parts).
draws: Graph: excess carrier concentration decaying with distance, with $L_p$ marked

questions.label: 18-19 5(d)
questions.text: A silicon n-channel JFET at $T = 300K$ has a gate doping concentration of $N_a = 10^{18}cm^{-3}$ and a channel doping concentration of $N_d = 2\times10^{16}cm^{-3}$. Determine the metallurgical channel thickness, $a$, such that the pinchoff voltage is $V_p = -2.50~V$.
draws: Diagram: n-channel JFET cross section with channel thickness and depletion regions

questions.label: 18-19 6(a)
questions.text: The parameters of an n-channel silicon JFET are $\mu_n = 1000~cm^2/V-s$, $N_d = 5\times10^{15}cm^{-3}$, $a = 0.50~\mu m$, and $L = 2~\mu m$. Determine the cutoff frequency.
questions.method: $f_T = g_m/(2\pi C_G)$ with $g_m(\max) = e\mu_nN_dWa/L$ and $C_G(\min) = \epsilon_sWL/a$: $f_T = e\mu_nN_da^2/(2\pi\epsilon_sL^2)$.

questions.label: 19-20 6(d)
questions.text: Does the doping level in the base of a BJT affect the emitter efficiency $\gamma_E$? If so, why?
questions.points: Yes: $\gamma = J_{nE}/(J_{nE} + J_{pE}) \approx 1/[1 + (N_B/N_E)(D_E/D_B)(x_B/x_E)]$; heavier base doping lowers $n_{B0} = n_i^2/N_B$, so fewer electrons are injected into the base relative to holes injected back into the emitter, and $\gamma$ falls; hence $N_E \gg N_B$.
draws: Diagram: minority carriers in emitter, base and collector
Graph: $\gamma$ against $N_B/N_E$

questions.label: 18-19 6(b)
questions.text: Design the ratio of emitter doping to base doping in order to achieve an emitter injection efficiency factor of $\gamma = 0.9967$. Assume a $npn$ bipolar transistor, and also consider $D_E = D_B$, $L_E = L_B$ and $x_E = X_B$.
questions.method: $\gamma = 1/[1 + (N_B/N_E)(D_E/D_B)(L_B/L_E)\tanh(x_B/L_B)/\tanh(x_E/L_E)]$; with equal $D$, $L$ and $x$: $\gamma = 1/(1 + N_B/N_E)$, so $N_E/N_B = 1/(1/\gamma - 1)$.
draws: Graph: emitter injection efficiency against the doping ratio

questions.label: 18-19 6(c)
questions.text: What is current crowding? What is the impact of current crowding in high power devices?
questions.points: Base current flows sideways under the emitter through the base resistance; the $I_Br_b$ drop makes $V_{BE}$ largest at the emitter edges, and injection $\propto e^{eV_{BE}/kT}$ crowds to the edges (18 mV doubles it). In power devices: local high current density, hot spots, second breakdown, lower gain; cured with narrow interdigitated emitters and ballast resistors.
draws: Diagram: npn cross section with lateral base current and injection crowded at the emitter edges
Diagram: interdigitated emitter and base fingers

questions.label: 20-21 1(c)
questions.text: Determine the number of quantum states(cm$^{-3}$) in silicon between $E_c$ and $E_c$+$kT$ at $T = 300$ K.
questions.method: Integrate the density of states $g_c(E) = 4\pi(2m_n^*)^{3/2}\sqrt{E - E_c}/h^3$ from $E_c$ to $E_c + kT$: $N = \frac{4\pi(2m_n^*)^{3/2}}{h^3}\cdot\frac23(kT)^{3/2}$.
draws: Graph: density of states with the shaded strip

questions.label: 18-19 7(a)
questions.text: Define the density of states and carrier concentration.
questions.points: Density of states $g(E)$: allowed states per unit energy per unit volume, $g_c = 4\pi(2m_n^*)^{3/2}\sqrt{E - E_c}/h^3$. Carrier concentration: free carriers per unit volume, $n_0 = \int g_cf_F\,dE = N_ce^{-(E_c - E_F)/kT}$.
draws: Graph: density of states in the conduction band of Si
compare: Density of states vs carrier concentration: states available vs states filled

questions.label: 18-19 7(c)
questions.text: What is electron-effective mass? Two possible conduction bands in the E versus k diagram are given in Figure 1. State which band will result in the heavier electron effective mass;state why.
questions.points: Effective mass: the mass that makes Newton's law work for an electron in the crystal, including the lattice forces: $1/m^* = (1/\hbar^2)d^2E/dk^2$. Band B is flatter (smaller curvature), so it gives the heavier effective mass (about 2.4 times band A from the figure).
draws: Graph: E-k diagram of bands A and B (Figure 1)
Graph: parabolic fits of bands A and B with their curvatures
compare: Band A vs band B: larger curvature, lighter mass vs flatter, heavier mass

questions.label: 18-19 7(d)
questions.text: Using the necessary theorem explains how band structure is formed of a particular solid-state material.
questions.points: Isolated atoms have discrete levels; brought together, wave functions overlap and Pauli forces each level to split into $N$ levels, forming bands. Bloch's theorem $\psi = u(x)e^{jkx}$ in the periodic Kronig-Penney potential gives $P'\sin\alpha a/\alpha a + \cos\alpha a = \cos ka$: allowed where the left side lies within $\pm1$, so allowed bands separated by forbidden gaps.
draws: Diagram: splitting of atomic levels into bands as atoms come together
Graph: Kronig-Penney function with allowed and forbidden bands
Graph: E-k diagram from the Kronig-Penney model

questions.label: 20-21 2(c)
questions.text: Using the expression for $V_{bi}$, find the width of the depletion region.\
questions.outline: Charge density $-eN_a$, $+eN_d$; integrate Poisson once with $E = 0$ at both edges; continuity gives $N_ax_p = N_dx_n$; integrate again for the potential; $V_{bi} = \phi(x_n)$; substitute $x_p = N_dx_n/N_a$; solve for $x_n$, $x_p$; add for $W$.
draws: Diagram: PN junction with its space charge region
Graph: charge density, field and potential across an abrupt junction

questions.label: 20-21 6(d)
questions.text: A silicon PN junction at $T = 300$ K with zero applied bias has doping concentration of $N_d = 5\times10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$ and $N_a = 5\times10^{15}$ cm$^{-3}$. Determine built-in potential, space charge width and electric field at metallurgical region ($\epsilon_t = 11.7$ *[sic: should be $\epsilon_r = 11.7$]*)
questions.method: $V_{bi} = V_t\ln(N_aN_d/n_i^2)$; $W = \{(2\epsilon_sV_{bi}/e)[(N_a + N_d)/(N_aN_d)]\}^{1/2}$; $x_n = WN_a/(N_a + N_d)$; $E_{max} = -eN_dx_n/\epsilon_s$.

questions.label: 19-20 4(c)
questions.text: For a pn junction with $N_a = 1.5\times10^{18}$cm$^{-3}$, $N_d = 1.5\times10^{16}$cm$^{-3}$ and $n_i = 2\times10^{10}$cm$^{-3}$ (i) calculate the built-in potential barrier $V_{bi}$ (ii) calculate the depletion region with *[sic: should be width]* and $E_{max}$ (Assume $\epsilon_s = 11.7\epsilon_o$) and (iii) what will be the width at liquid nitrogen temperature (80K).
questions.method: $V_{bi} = V_t\ln(N_aN_d/n_i^2)$; $W = \{(2\epsilon_sV_{bi}/e)[(N_a + N_d)/(N_aN_d)]\}^{1/2}$; $E_{max} = -eN_dx_n/\epsilon_s$; at 80 K scale $n_i$ by $(T/300)^{3/2}e^{-E_g/2k(1/T - 1/300)}$ and $V_t$ by $T/300$.
draws: Graph: space charge and field triangles at 300 K and 80 K

questions.label: 19-20 5(d)
questions.text: An abrupt silicon pn junction has dopant concentrations of $N_a = 2\times10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$ and $N_d = 2\times10^{15}$ cm$^{-3}$ at $T = 300$ K. Calculate: (i) $V_{bi}$ (ii) $W$ at $V_R = 0$ and $V_R = 8$ V and (iii) the maximum electric field in the space charge region at $V_R = 0$ and $V_R = 8$ V
questions.method: $V_{bi} = V_t\ln(N_aN_d/n_i^2)$; $W = \{(2\epsilon_s(V_{bi} + V_R)/e)[(N_a + N_d)/(N_aN_d)]\}^{1/2}$; $|E_{max}| = 2(V_{bi} + V_R)/W$ at $V_R = 0$ and 8 V.
draws: Graph: field triangles at 0 and 8 V reverse bias

questions.label: 18-19 TT2 8(a)
questions.text: A silicon pn junction at T = 300 K with zero applied bias has doping concentrations of $N_d = 5\times10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$ and $N_a = 5\times10^{20}$ *[sic: should be $5\times10^{15}$]* cm$^{-3}$. Determine $x_n$, $x_p$ and $W$.
questions.method: $V_{bi} = (kT/e)\ln(N_aN_d/n_i^2)$; $x_n = [(2\epsilon_sV_{bi}/e)(N_a/N_d)/(N_a + N_d)]^{1/2}$, $x_p$ with $N_d/N_a$; $W = x_n + x_p$; check $N_ax_p = N_dx_n$.

questions.label: 20-21 1(a)
questions.text: Sketch the position of Fermi level in Si at 300 K as a function of doping concentration.
questions.points: $E_F - E_{Fi} = kT\ln(N_d/n_i)$ in n-type, $E_{Fi} - E_F = kT\ln(N_a/n_i)$ in p-type; on a log doping axis both are straight lines of 0.06 eV per decade (0.23, 0.35, 0.47, 0.53 eV at $10^{14}$ to $10^{19}$ cm$^{-3}$); $E_F$ moves towards $E_c$ with donors and $E_v$ with acceptors, reaching the band edge at degeneracy.

Diagram: band diagrams of intrinsic, n-type and p-type Si
Graph: Fermi level against doping at 300 K

questions.label: 20-21 TT2 8(c)
questions.text: Sketch $E_c$, $E_v$, $E_{Fi}$ and $E_F$ for a p type extrinsic semiconductor.
draws: Diagram: $E_c$, $E_v$, $E_{Fi}$ and $E_F$ of p-type Si, $E_F$ below $E_{Fi}$ near $E_v$

questions.label: 19-20 TT1 7(b)
questions.text: With proper equation and graph, explain variation of Fermi energy level in extrinsic semiconductor.
questions.points: $E_F - E_{Fi} = kT\ln(n_0/n_i)$, $E_{Fi} - E_F = kT\ln(p_0/n_i)$, or $E_c - E_F = kT\ln(N_c/N_d)$, $E_F - E_v = kT\ln(N_v/N_a)$: $E_F$ moves 0.06 eV per decade of doping towards the majority band edge, and back towards $E_{Fi}$ as $T$ rises and $n_i$ grows; freeze-out at very low $T$.

Graph: Fermi level against temperature for several dopings

questions.label: 18-19 TT2 8(b)
questions.text: Determine the position of the Fermi level with respect to the valence band energy in p type GaAs at T = 300 K. The doping concentrations are [unclear: $N_a$] $= 5\times10^{19}$ *[sic: should be $5\times10^{16}$]* cm$^{-3}$ and $N_d = 10^{15}$ *[sic: should be $4\times10^{15}$]* cm$^{-3}$.
questions.method: Compensated p-type: $p_0 = N_a - N_d$; $E_F - E_v = kT\ln(N_v/p_0)$ with $N_v = 7.0\times10^{18}$ cm$^{-3}$ for GaAs.
draws: Diagram: GaAs band diagram with the Fermi level near the valence band

questions.label: 20-21 3(c)
questions.text: Define drift mobility. Explain the mechanism of carrier scattering in semiconductor materials and significance of $\tau$.
questions.points: Drift mobility $\mu = |v_d|/E = e\tau/m^*$. Scattering by lattice vibrations ($\mu_L \propto T^{-3/2}$) and ionized impurities ($\mu_I \propto T^{3/2}/N_I$), combined by $1/\mu = 1/\mu_L + 1/\mu_I$. The mean free time $\tau$ (about $10^{-13}$ s) sets the mobility and so the conductivity.
draws: Diagram: electron path with and without a field
Diagram: lattice and ionized impurity scattering
compare: Lattice vs ionized impurity scattering: grows with temperature, $\mu_L \propto T^{-3/2}$ vs weakens with temperature, $\mu_I \propto T^{3/2}/N_I$

questions.label: 20-21 4(a)
questions.text: Explain the effects of temperature on carrier mobility inside a semiconductor.
questions.points: Lattice scattering grows with $T$, so $\mu_L \propto T^{-3/2}$ falls; impurity scattering weakens as carriers get faster, so $\mu_I \propto T^{3/2}/N_I$ rises; by Matthiessen's rule impurity scattering dominates at low $T$ (mobility rises), lattice at high $T$ (mobility falls); heavier doping lowers the curve.
draws: Graph: mobility against temperature, log-log

questions.label: 19-20 3(d)
questions.text: Consider a compensated n-type silicon at $T = 300$ K with a conductivity of $\rho$ *[sic: should be $\sigma$]* $= 16~(\Omega-\text{cm})^{-1}$ and an acceptor doping concentration of $10^{17}$ cm$^{-3}$. Determine the doner *[sic: should be donor]* concentration and the electron mobility.
questions.method: $\sigma = e\mu_n(N_d - N_a)$ with $\mu_n$ read at $N_I = N_d + N_a$ from the mobility curve; trial and error ($\rho$ printed for $\sigma$).
draws: Graph: electron mobility against total impurity with the trial points

questions.label: 19-20 4(a)
questions.text: With proper graphs, explain how mobility is affected by temperature and doping concentration.
questions.points: Lattice scattering $\mu_L \propto T^{-3/2}$, impurity scattering $\mu_I \propto T^{3/2}/N_I$, $1/\mu = 1/\mu_L + 1/\mu_I$: $\mu$ rises with $T$ at low $T$, falls at high $T$; flat at low doping (about 1350 and 480 cm$^2$/V s in Si), falls steeply above $10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$ of total ionized impurity.
draws: Graph: mobility against temperature, log-log
Graph: electron and hole mobility against doping
compare: Lattice vs ionized impurity scattering: grows with temperature, $\mu_L \propto T^{-3/2}$ vs weakens with temperature, $\mu_I \propto T^{3/2}/N_I$

questions.label: 18-19 TT2 8(c)
questions.text: Silicon at T = 300 K is doped with impurity concentrations of Nd = 5 × 1016 *[sic: should be $10^{16}$]* /cm3 and Na = 2 × 1016 *[sic: should be $10^{16}$]* /cm3. (a) What are the electron and hole mobilities? (b) Determine the conductivity and resistivity of the [unclear: material].
questions.method: Mobility from the total $N_I = N_d + N_a$ (Neamen Fig. 5.3); $n_0 = N_d - N_a$; $\sigma = e(\mu_nn_0 + \mu_pp_0) \approx e\mu_nn_0$; $\rho = 1/\sigma$.
draws: Graph: electron and hole mobility against total impurity concentration
compare: Net vs total doping: $N_d - N_a$ sets $n_0$ vs $N_d + N_a$ sets the mobility

questions.label: 19-20 1(a)
questions.text: Describe three classifications of solids-amorphous, polycrystalline, and single crystal.
questions.points: Amorphous: order only within a few atomic distances, no grains (glass, a-Si). Polycrystalline: high order inside grains of different orientation, separated by grain boundaries (polysilicon gates). Single crystal: one lattice through the whole volume, no grain boundaries, best electrical properties (Si wafers).
draws: Diagram: atoms in amorphous, polycrystalline and single-crystal solids
compare: Amorphous vs polycrystalline vs single crystal: short-range order only vs ordered grains with boundaries vs one lattice throughout

questions.label: 19-20 1(b)
questions.text: The lattice constant of a face-centered cubic lattice is 0.425 nm. Determine the (i) effective number of atoms per unit cell (ii) volume density of atoms
questions.method: fcc: 8 corner atoms shared by 8 cells, 6 face atoms shared by 2: $8\times\frac18 + 6\times\frac12 = 4$; volume density $= 4/a^3$ with $a$ in cm.
questions.answer: (i) 4 atoms per unit cell; (ii) $5.21\times10^{22}$ cm$^{-3}$ ($a = 0.425$ nm)
draws: Diagram: fcc unit cell with corner and face atoms

questions.label: 19-20 1(c)
questions.text: If the free electrons in a semiconductor have effective mass $m_c = 0.1m_o$, where $m_o$ is the mass of the electron in vacuum, what is their average speed at $T = 300K$? If the free holes in the same material have effective mass $m_v = 1.5m_o$, what is their average speed at the same temperature? Assume a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of the electron energies.
questions.method: Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution; mean speed $\bar v = \sqrt{8kT/\pi m^*}$ (rms $\sqrt{3kT/m^*}$ for comparison) with $m^* = 0.1m_0$ and $1.5m_0$.
draws: Graph: Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distributions for the two masses

questions.label: 21-22 7(f)
questions.text: Silicon atoms, at a concentration of 7 $\times$ 10$^{15}$ cm$^{-3}$, are added to gallium arsenide. Assume that the silicon atoms act as fully ionized dopant atoms and that 5 percent of the concentration added replaces gallium atoms and 95 percent replaces arsenic atoms. Let T = 300 K and GaAs has an intrinsic concentration of 1.8x10$^{6}$ cm $^{-3}$. (i) Determine the donor and acceptor concentration. (ii) Is the material n-type or p-type? (iii) Calculate the electron and hole concentration. (iv) Determine the position of the Fermi level with respect to $E_{Fi}$.
questions.method: Si on Ga sites are donors, on As sites acceptors: $N_d = 0.05N$, $N_a = 0.95N$; $N_a > N_d$ so p-type; $p_0 = (N_a - N_d)/2 + \sqrt{((N_a - N_d)/2)^2 + n_i^2}$, $n_0 = n_i^2/p_0$; $E_{Fi} - E_F = kT\ln(p_0/n_i)$.
draws: Diagram: Si on Ga and As sites in GaAs
Diagram: GaAs band diagram with $E_F$ below $E_{Fi}$
compare: Si on a Ga site vs Si on an As site: donor (+) vs acceptor (−)

questions.label: 20-21 2(a)
questions.text: Draw energy band diagram of a compensated semiconductor.
questions.points: Both donors and acceptors in one region; donor electrons fall into the acceptor states, so donors are ionized (+) and acceptors filled (−). For $N_d > N_a$: n-type, $n_0 \approx N_d - N_a$, $E_F$ above $E_{Fi}$; for $N_a > N_d$: p-type; for $N_a = N_d$: behaves intrinsic.
draws: Diagram: band diagrams of a compensated semiconductor for three cases
Graph: Fermi level against acceptor concentration

questions.label: 20-21 TT2 8(b)
questions.text: What is compensated semiconductor?
questions.points: Both donors and acceptors in the same region; donor electrons fill the acceptor states, so only the net doping gives carriers: $n_0 \approx N_d - N_a$ if $N_d > N_a$, $p_0 \approx N_a - N_d$ if $N_a > N_d$, intrinsic-like if equal.
draws: Diagram: band diagrams of a compensated semiconductor for three cases

questions.label: 19-20 2(d)
questions.text: Sketch and briefly describe energy band diagram of compensated semiconductor.
questions.points: Donor electrons drop into acceptor levels, so all dopants are ionized; $N_d > N_a$: n-type, $n_0 \approx N_d - N_a$, $E_F$ above $E_{Fi}$; $N_a > N_d$: p-type, $p_0 \approx N_a - N_d$, $E_F$ below $E_{Fi}$; $N_d = N_a$: intrinsic-like; mobility set by $N_d + N_a$.
draws: Diagram: band diagrams of a compensated semiconductor for three cases

questions.label: 19-20 3(a)
questions.text: Sketch and explain density of states functions, Fermi distribution, and carrier concentration distribution curves of n-type material in a single graph.
questions.points: $g_c \propto \sqrt{E - E_c}$, $g_v \propto \sqrt{E_v - E}$, zero in the gap; $f_F$ with $E_F$ above $E_{Fi}$ for n-type; $n(E) = g_cf_F$ and $p(E) = g_v(1 - f_F)$ peak $kT/2$ inside each band; areas $n_0 \gg p_0$.
draws: Graph: density of states, Fermi function and carrier distributions of n-type on one energy axis

questions.label: 19-20 3(b)
questions.text: Explain how barrier potential maintains equilibrium p, n regions.
questions.points: Diffusion uncovers ions, giving a field from n to p and a barrier $V_{bi} = (kT/e)\ln(N_aN_d/n_i^2)$; drift cancels diffusion for each carrier ($J_n = J_p = 0$); only $e^{-eV_{bi}/kT}$ of the majority carriers cross, $n_{p0} = n_{n0}e^{-eV_{bi}/kT}$; $E_F$ flat.
draws: Diagram: equilibrium band diagram of a pn junction
Diagram: drift and diffusion fluxes across the space charge region

questions.label: 19-20 3(c)
questions.text: Explain dielectric relaxation time. Find the equation for dielectric relaxation.
questions.outline: Continuity $\nabla\cdot J = -\partial\rho/\partial t$; Ohm $J = \sigma E$; Poisson $\nabla\cdot E = \rho/\epsilon$; $d\rho/dt + (\sigma/\epsilon)\rho = 0$; $\rho = \rho(0)e^{-t/\tau_d}$, $\tau_d = \epsilon/\sigma$ (0.539 ps for $10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$ Si).
draws: Diagram: net charge drawing in majority carriers
Graph: exponential decay of the net charge

questions.label: 19-20 4(b)
questions.text: Define ambipolar transport. Find ambipolar transport equation. Hence show that diffuse and drift behavior of excess majority carrier is determined by excess minority carrier.
questions.outline: Continuity for holes and electrons; drift-diffusion fluxes; time-dependent diffusion equations; excess form with $\delta n = \delta p$, $g_n = g_p$, $R_n = R_p$; multiply by $\mu_nn$ and $\mu_pp$ and add so $\partial E/\partial x$ cancels; divide: $D'$, $\mu'$; low injection: $D' = D_n$, $\mu' = \mu_n$ in p-type ($D_p$, $-\mu_p$ in n-type), so the majority carriers follow the minority carriers.
draws: Diagram: excess electrons and holes held together by their internal field

questions.label: 19-20 TT2 8(b)
questions.text: Define ambipolar transport. Find ambipolar transport equation. Hence show that diffuse and drift behavior of excess majority carrier is determined by excess minority carrier.
questions.outline: Continuity for holes and electrons; drift-diffusion fluxes; time-dependent diffusion equations; excess form with $\delta n = \delta p$, $g_n = g_p$, $R_n = R_p$; multiply by $\mu_nn$ and $\mu_pp$ and add so $\partial E/\partial x$ cancels; divide: $D'$, $\mu'$; low injection: $D' = D_n$, $\mu' = \mu_n$ in p-type ($D_p$, $-\mu_p$ in n-type), so the majority carriers follow the minority carriers.
draws: Diagram: excess electrons and holes held together by their internal field

questions.label: 19-20 4(d)
questions.text: With proper graphs, explain time and spatial dependence of excess carrier concentration.
questions.points: Uniform: $\delta p = \delta p(0)e^{-t/\tau_{p0}}$ after the light stops, $g'\tau_{p0}(1 - e^{-t/\tau_{p0}})$ after it starts; steady injection: $\delta p = \delta p(0)e^{-x/L_p}$, $L_p = \sqrt{D_p\tau_{p0}}$; a pulse is a Gaussian that spreads ($4D_pt$), decays ($e^{-t/\tau_{p0}}$) and drifts at $\mu_pE_0$.
draws: Graph: time decay and build-up of a uniform excess
Graph: steady-state decay from a surface
Graph: excess carrier pulse at three times with and without a field

questions.label: 19-20 5(c)
questions.text: Consider an n-type semiconductor at $T = 300$ K with carrier concentrations of $n_o = 10^{15}$ cm$^{-3}$, $n_i = 10^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$ and $p_o = 10^5$ cm$^{-3}$. In non-equilibrium, assume that the excess carrier concentrations are $\delta n = \delta p = 10^{-13}$ *[sic: should be $10^{13}$]* cm$^{-3}$. Calculate the quasi-Fermi energy levels.
questions.method: $E_{Fn} - E_{Fi} = kT\ln[(n_0 + \delta n)/n_i]$, $E_{Fi} - E_{Fp} = kT\ln[(p_0 + \delta p)/n_i]$ with $\delta n = \delta p = 10^{13}$ cm$^{-3}$ (printed $10^{-13}$).
draws: Diagram: band diagram in equilibrium and with quasi-Fermi levels

questions.label: 20-21 4(c)
questions.text: Show the four operating modes of a bipolar transistor as a function of $V_{BE}$ and $V_{CB}$. Draw the minority carrier distribution of the four modes of a NPN transistor with proper labelling of all the quantities.
questions.points: Forward active ($V_{BE} > 0$, $V_{CB} > 0$), saturation (both junctions forward), cutoff (both reverse), inverse active; a forward junction raises the minority edge value by $e^{V/V_t}$, a reverse one takes it to 0; draw the base, emitter and collector minority profiles for each mode with the edge values.
draws: Diagram: NPN structure and the four modes on the $V_{BE}$–$V_{CB}$ plane
Graph: minority carrier distributions in the four modes

questions.label: 19-20 6(b)
questions.text: Determine the mode of operation of an NPN BJT with $\beta \approx 450$, if it is known that: (i) $V_{BE} = 0.7V$, $V_{CE} = 5.2V$ (ii) $V_{BE} = 0.7V$, $V_{CE} = 0.2V$ (iii) $V_{BE} = 0.8V$, $V_{BC} = 0.3V$ (iv) $V_{BE} = -0.8V$, $V_{BC} = 0.7V$ (v) $I_C = 455mA$, $I_B = 1mA$ (vi) $I_C = 455mA$, $I_E = 502mA$
questions.method: $V_{BC} = V_{BE} - V_{CE}$; B-E and B-C forward or reverse decide the mode; from currents compare $I_C/I_B$ with $\beta$ ($I_B = I_E - I_C$).
questions.answer: i forward active; ii saturation; iii saturation (soft); iv inverse active; v forward active; vi saturation ($I_C/I_B = 9.7$)
draws: Diagram: four modes on the $V_{BE}$–$V_{BC}$ plane with the cases

questions.label: 19-20 6(c)
questions.text: Mention some advantages of using MOSFET.
questions.points: Insulated gate: very high input impedance, voltage control, almost no drive power; CMOS draws almost no static power; small, simple, dense; majority carrier, no storage delay; mobility falls with temperature, no thermal runaway, easy paralleling; good bidirectional switch.

questions.label: 19-20 TT2 8(c)
questions.text: Briefly describe different types of generation and recombination processes. Use appropriate diagram if necessary.
questions.points: Band to band: $h\nu \ge E_g$ or heat makes a pair, an electron falling into a hole emits a photon, rate $\alpha_r(np - n_i^2)$, GaAs. SRH: traps in the gap capture and emit electrons and holes (four processes), $R = C_nC_pN_t(np - n_i^2)/[C_n(n + n') + C_p(p + p')]$, non-radiative, dominant in Si. Auger: energy to a third carrier, heavy doping; inverse is impact ionization. Surface recombination through dangling-bond traps.
draws: Diagram: band-to-band, trap (SRH) and Auger processes
compare: Band-to-band vs SRH recombination: direct, radiative, GaAs vs through traps, heat, Si

questions.label: 20-21 1(b)
questions.text: How do you define a minority carrier? Why does it diffuse? What is Poisson's equation and why is it important in PN junction?
questions.points: Minority carrier: the less numerous carrier ($p_{n0} = n_i^2/N_d$). It diffuses because random thermal motion in a concentration gradient gives a net flow from high to low; injected minority carriers recombine as they spread, so their current is diffusion current. Poisson: $d^2\phi/dx^2 = -\rho/\epsilon_s$ links the space charge to the field and potential, giving $E_{max}$, $V_{bi}$ and $W$ of a junction.
draws: Diagram: diffusion of carriers down a concentration gradient
Graph: charge density, field and potential of a PN junction
compare: Minority vs majority carriers: fewer, set by $n_i^2/N$, move by diffusion vs more, set by the doping, carry drift current

questions.label: 21-22 7(b)
questions.text: Explain Ionization Energy.
questions.points: Energy to free a donor's fifth electron ($E_c - E_d$) or to fill an acceptor's missing bond ($E_a - E_v$), leaving a fixed ion and a free carrier. Hydrogen model: $E_{ion} = 13.6(m^*/m_0)/\epsilon_r^2 = 25.8$ meV in Si; measured 0.045 eV (P, B), 0.05 eV (As); close to $kT$, so dopants are fully ionized at 300 K.
draws: Diagram: donor electron orbiting its ion in the Si lattice
Diagram: donor and acceptor ionization on the band diagram
compare: Donor vs acceptor: gives an electron, level near $E_c$, becomes + vs takes an electron, level near $E_v$, becomes −

questions.label: 20-21 1(d)
questions.text: A Si sample is doped with $N_d = 1\times10^{15}$ cm$^{-3}$ of As atoms. Calculate the electron and hole concentrations and the position of Fermi level position (w.r.t. $E_c/E_v$) at 300 K, assuming full ionization. Justify the assumption by calculating the probability of doner *[sic: should be donor]* states being occupied by electrons and therefore not ionized (assume, $E_C - E_D = 50$ meV). Repeat the above calculations for $T = 30$ K and comment on the values and assumptions. [$N_c = 2.8\times10^{19}$ cm$^{-3}$, for Si].
questions.method: $n_0 = N_d$, $p_0 = n_i^2/n_0$; $E_c - E_F = kT\ln(N_c/n_0)$, $E_F - E_v = E_g - (E_c - E_F)$; fraction on donors $1/[1 + (N_c/2N_d)e^{-(E_c - E_d)/kT}]$.
draws: Diagram: band diagram of the As-doped sample
Graph: ionized fraction and Fermi level against temperature

questions.label: 20-21 6(b)
questions.text: Briefly explain the terms complete ionization and freeze out. Can we achieve complete ionization in room temperature? Prove your answer.
questions.outline: Donor occupation with the factor $\tfrac12$; non-degenerate: $n_d \approx 2N_de^{-(E_d - E_F)/kT}$; $n_0 = N_ce^{-(E_c - E_F)/kT}$; the ratio cancels $E_F$; fraction $1/[1 + (N_c/2N_d)e^{-(E_c - E_d)/kT}]$; 0.4 % for P in Si at $10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$, 300 K.
draws: Diagram: donor states at 0 K, low temperature and 300 K
Graph: $n_0/N_d$ against temperature
compare: Complete ionization vs freeze-out: every donor gives its electron, $n_0 = N_d$ vs electrons fall back to donors at low $T$, $n_0 < N_d$

questions.label: 20-21 TT1 7(a)
questions.text: What fraction of donor or acceptor states are ionized at room temperature?
questions.points: Essentially all (complete ionization) because $E_c - E_d = 0.045$ eV $< 2kT$ and $N_c \gg N_d$; fraction still on donors $1/[1 + (N_c/2N_d)e^{-(E_c - E_d)/kT}] = 0.40$ % for P at $10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$ (99.6 % ionized); B acceptors at $10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$ about 97.9 % ionized ($g = 4$).
draws: Diagram: donor states at 0 K, low temperature and 300 K

questions.label: 20-21 TT1 7(b)
questions.text: What is the probability function of electron occupying the donor state??
questions.points: $f_d = 1/[1 + \tfrac12\exp((E_d - E_F)/kT)]$, $n_d = N_d - N_d^+$; the $\tfrac12$ ($1/g$, $g = 2$) comes from the two spin states of a donor level that holds only one electron; $f_d = 2/3$ at $E_d = E_F$.
draws: Graph: Fermi-Dirac function and donor occupation function

questions.label: 20-21 3(b)
questions.text: Sketch Energy-band diagram of a PN junction in thermal equilibrium and show P region, N region, $E_C$, $E_V$, $E_F$, $E_{Fi}$, $e\phi_{Fn}$, $e\phi_{Fp}$ and $eV_{bi}$.
questions.points: $E_F$ flat through the device; on the P side $E_F$ is $e\phi_{Fp} = kT\ln(N_a/n_i)$ below $E_{Fi}$, on the N side $e|\phi_{Fn}| = kT\ln(N_d/n_i)$ above it; the bands are higher on the P side by $eV_{bi}$ and bend only inside the space charge region; $V_{bi} = |\phi_{Fp}| + |\phi_{Fn}|$.
draws: Diagram: p and n band diagrams before contact
Diagram: equilibrium band diagram of a PN junction with all labels

questions.label: 20-21 4(d)
questions.text: Consider a PN junction at room temperature with $n_i = 1.5\times10^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$, assume doping in N side is $1\times10^{6}$ cm$^{-3}$ *[sic: should be $1\times10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$]*. What will be the minority carrier hole concentrations at the edge in N side if forward bias and reverse bias of 0.7 V is applied? Do the same for majority carrier electron concentration in N side.
questions.method: $p_{n0} = n_i^2/N_d$; law of the junction $p_n(x_n) = p_{n0}e^{eV_a/kT}$ with $V_a = +0.7$ and $-0.7$ V; $n_n = N_d + \delta p$ (neutrality); check low injection.
questions.answer: $p_{n0} = 2.25\times10^4$; forward: $p_n = 1.23\times10^{16}$, $n_n = 2.23\times10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$ (low injection violated); reverse: $p_n \approx 0$, $n_n \approx 10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$
draws: Diagram: band diagrams under forward and reverse bias
Graph: hole and electron concentrations on the n side

questions.label: 20-21 5(a)
questions.text: Write the ambipolar equation for $g' = 0$ for n type semiconductor with constant electric field $E_0$. At time $t = 0$, a number of electron-hole pair is generated at $x = 0$. Sketch excess electron concentration as a function of distance at different time.
questions.points: For n-type at low injection the ambipolar equation uses $D_p$, $\mu_p$, $\tau_{p0}$: $D_p\,\partial^2\delta p/\partial x^2 - \mu_pE_0\,\partial\delta p/\partial x - \delta p/\tau_{p0} = \partial\delta p/\partial t$. A pulse at $x = 0$ becomes a Gaussian that spreads, shrinks by recombination and drifts in the direction of $E_0$ at $\mu_pE_0$.
draws: Diagram: excess electrons and holes held together by their field
Graph: excess carrier pulse at three times, with and without a field

questions.label: 20-21 5(b)
questions.text: For NPN transistor, plot minority carrier concentration in base, emitter, and collector as a function of space. What are the minority carrier concentrations at the boundaries of base, emitter, and collector?
questions.points: Forward active: base electrons fall almost linearly from $n_{B0}e^{V_{BE}/V_t}$ at the emitter edge to about 0 at the collector edge; emitter holes fall from $p_{E0}e^{V_{BE}/V_t}$ to $p_{E0}$; collector holes rise from about 0 to $p_{C0}$.
draws: Diagram: NPN in forward-active mode with depletion layers
Graph: minority carrier concentrations in emitter, base and collector

questions.label: 20-21 6(a)
questions.text: Draw the schematic of a double-gate MOS structure. What are the benefits of such structure over single-gate MOS?
questions.points: A thin (undoped) silicon body between two thin gate oxides with a gate on each side, n$^+$ source and drain (FinFET is its practical form). Benefits: better gate control of the channel, much smaller short-channel effects (DIBL, $V_T$ roll-off), near-ideal subthreshold swing, low leakage, more drive current, no doping fluctuation.
draws: Diagram: single-gate, planar double-gate and FinFET schematics
Graph: subthreshold current of single and double gate
compare: Single-gate vs double-gate MOSFET: gate controls one surface, short-channel effects vs gate on both sides, better control, near-ideal swing

questions.label: 20-21 6(c)
questions.text: Explain production of inverse layer at oxide and semiconductor layer with proper sketches of energy band diagram.
questions.points: Positive gate voltage on a p-type body repels holes and bends the bands down by $e\phi_s$: depletion for $\phi_s < \phi_{fp}$, intrinsic surface at $\phi_s = \phi_{fp}$, n-type inversion layer once $E_{Fi}$ falls below $E_F$; threshold at $\phi_s = 2\phi_{fp}$ ($n_s = N_a$), depletion width at its maximum $x_{dT}$.
draws: Diagram: band diagrams of a p-type MOS structure from depletion to inversion
Diagram: charge distribution at threshold inversion

questions.label: 20-21 TT1 7(c)
questions.text: What are n, p, n$_o$ and p$_o$?
questions.points: $n_0$, $p_0$: thermal-equilibrium concentrations, $n_0p_0 = n_i^2$; $n = n_0 + \delta n$, $p = p_0 + \delta p$: total concentrations including excess carriers from light or injection, may vary with time and position.
draws: Diagram: n-type sample in equilibrium and under light
compare: Equilibrium vs total concentration: $n_0$ fixed by doping and $T$ vs $n = n_0 + \delta n$ out of equilibrium

questions.label: 20-21 TT1 7(d)
questions.text: Can Si be used as a donor? How?
questions.points: Yes, in a III-V compound such as GaAs: Si (4 valence electrons) on a Ga site (3) has one left over and is a donor (0.0058 eV); on an As site (5) it is an acceptor, so Si is amphoteric, mostly a donor in GaAs; in Si it is the host atom.
draws: Diagram: Si on a Ga site, on an As site and in silicon

questions.label: 20-21 TT2 8(d)
questions.text: Can Si be used as a donor? How?
questions.points: Yes, in GaAs: Si on a Ga site has one valence electron more than Ga and gives it to the conduction band (0.0058 eV); on an As site it is an acceptor (amphoteric), mostly a donor; in Si it is the host.
draws: Diagram: Si on a Ga site, on an As site and in silicon

questions.label: 20-21 TT2 8(e)
questions.text: What is degenerated semiconductor?
questions.points: So heavily doped ($\gtrsim 10^{18}$ cm$^{-3}$ in Si) that the impurity band overlaps the band edge and $E_F$ lies inside the conduction band ($n_0 > N_c$) or the valence band ($p_0 > N_v$); Boltzmann and $n_0p_0 = n_i^2$ fail; used in tunnel diodes and ohmic contacts.
draws: Diagram: non-degenerate and degenerate n- and p-type band diagrams
compare: Degenerate vs non-degenerate: $E_F$ inside a band, metal-like vs $E_F$ in the gap, $n_0p_0 = n_i^2$ holds
